summary:
Loreto is a department of Peru and stands under the national framework: Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

No trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement finding for Loreto appears in the sources. Every attached item is national in scope, and as national law the restrictions below apply in Loreto.

Facility access is restricted by statute. On 20 February 2025 the Congress Commission on Women and Family approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457, which bar entry to public sanitary facilities destined to the sex opposite to one's birth sex. Exceptions cover custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12, or a disabled person, and the measure requires unambiguous signage. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory and warned that security staff would judge people by personal criteria, including requests to produce a DNI.

The plenary approved the law on 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote. Its article 5 bars from public sanitary facilities anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients, or people with specific needs.

IDEHPUCP analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte finds that the measure implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable biological sex, and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination. The same analysis records that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage.

Violence against trans people is documented and rising. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report recorded 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with trans women the most affected and hate crimes increasing. In February 2023 the trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, was kidnapped in central Lima and murdered in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots at the hands of the 'Los Gallegos' gang; the body showed gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting, indicating extreme hate.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern behind the departmental picture pairs legislative hostility with partial judicial protection. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Enforcement of the bathroom restriction reaches private as well as public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'. IDEHPUCP also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.
localsOnly:
Congress has banned inclusive language, and the April 2025 legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The same package again rejected equal marriage.

Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Residents enforcing or contesting the facility rule face a documented enforcement gap: the national consumer-protection body declined to act on a trans woman's complaint against a private gym applying the policy, which leaves private venues largely unaccountable for how they screen users.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source records how article 5 is enforced within Loreto: whether security staff at Iquitos or departmental facilities request identity documents, which venues post the required signage, or whether any complaint has been filed in the department. This is unresolved rather than established as absent.

No hate-crime or killing figures for Loreto appear in the inventory. The 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases are national totals covering 2020 to 2023 and are not disaggregated by department, so the department's share of that violence is not sourced.

Whether the June 2024 revision of health guidance and the July 2025 constitutional ruling are applied by Loreto's regional health and judicial authorities is not sourced.

The sources do not state whether the exceptions in article 5 have been invoked in Loreto, nor whether any regional authority has issued signage or implementing instructions under the April 2025 law.
